title: What Transfers in Models of Replication-Origin Firing: Pre-Registered Out-of-Sample Tests
content: Models of replication-origin firing in Saccharomyces cerevisiae are routinely fitted and judged on the data that shaped them. Here a mechanistic two-step model of origin firing, fitted to a checkpoint-mutant factorial, was frozen, deposited with a checksum, and tested against independent datasets under predictions written and hashed before each dataset was opened. Seven tests followed: five scored out of sample, one retrodiction and one prediction still untested. Successor models were frozen and tested the same way. The model described the genotypes it was fitted to, but its origin-level content failed on independent data: it overstated the wild-type timing spread about twofold, and a blind run on its own genotype factorial showed brake effects combining as a product rather than as a sequence. A hybrid that learned a firing rate for each of 409 confirmed origins from one laboratory's wild-type time course ranked another laboratory's origins at Spearman 0.86 and reproduced the timing compression caused by overexpression of six limiting initiation factors with no competition term. Every mechanistic layer subjected to independent predictive testing failed. A uniform step multiplier predicted that loss of the S-phase cyclin Clb5 would flatten the replication profile; the profile sharpened instead (slope 1.70; late origins lost 12.4 against 3.6 percentage points). Per-origin step sensitivities cut training error by a third but transferred worse than a single shared sensitivity. Origin timing is predictable from wild-type data alone; how perturbations act on it is origin-specific in ways that neither a global rule nor a free per-origin parameter captures. All models, predictions, hashes and results are deposited on Zenodo.
